title: Bound the nearest neighbour query in the resplit assignment loop, with identical output
body: **What changes.** One bound on the nearest neighbour query in `MLS_resplit`'s assignment loop, in `kdtree.h`, `kdtree.c` and `mesh_resplit.c`. What the bound does to a cube with the gate armed. Two bars per cube, before and after, each stacked: the part the change does not touch is the same height in both. **Why.** That loop keeps only the best and the second best distance and throws the index away, so a piece that cannot beat the second best need not be searched at all. **That the output does not move.** Six arms, three cubes, both gate settings: every file the run writes is byte identical to the unchanged binary's, 0 of 54, 244, 28, 171, 36 and 186 differing, and the number of queries is unchanged exactly, which is what makes this a pruning and not a different computation. **What it is worth**, with the gate armed: | cube | Resplit before, after | stage | cube before, after | cube | |---|---|---:|---|---:| | z09216_y03840_x03840 | 710.484 s, 130.983 | 5.424x | 817.0 s, 237.7 | 3.437x | | z09472_y02560_x02560 | 334.559 s, 100.074 | 3.343x | 412.5 s, 178.1 | 2.316x | | z09728_y03712_x02560 | 408.885 s, 113.803 | 3.593x | 488.5 s, 193.5 | 2.525x | **How to check it yourself.** Build this branch and `main`, run `cube_mesh` on the same cube with `BPA_GROW_WIND_TOL=0.45`, and compare the two output trees file by file. They should be equal. Then time them. **On the platform.** These measurements were taken on Linux, where this repository needs three further changes to build at all, which are a separate pull request of ours. **This change is not stacked on them**: it touches three files that are the same on every platform and applies to `main` as it stands. --- `MLS_resplit`'s assignment loop asks, for every parent point and every piece, a 1-NN query whose **index it throws away**: it keeps only the best and the second best distance. A piece that cannot beat the second best therefore cannot change anything the loop does, and need not be searched. This bounds that query. The delivered output does not move. ## What it is worth, on three grid cubes of PHerc. 0139 Two binaries built minutes apart by the same command from the same tree, differing only by this change and **neither carrying an instrumentation counter**. Three repeats of each arm, serial, nothing else on the machine, the two arms interleaved inside each repeat so drift falls on both. With the growth gate armed at 0.45: | cube | Resplit, before to after | stage | whole cube, before to after | cube | |---|---|---:|---|---:| | z09216_y03840_x03840 | 710.484 s to 130.983 | **5.424x** | 817.0 s to 237.7 | **3.437x** | | z09472_y02560_x02560 | 334.559 s to 100.074 | **3.343x** | 412.5 s to 178.1 | **2.316x** | | z09728_y03712_x02560 | 408.885 s to 113.803 | **3.593x** | 488.5 s to 193.5 | **2.525x** | With the gate off, where the search is a third of a cube rather than most of it, the same change is worth 1.304, 1.156 and 1.174 times on the stage and 1.099, 1.044 and 1.052 on the cube. **Both numbers are given because neither is the answer on its own.** The stage figure says what the change does to the code it touches; the cube figure says what a user gets; and the difference between them is the stage's share of the cube, 86.96, 81.11 and 83.70 per cent with the gate armed and about a third with it off. We are not averaging the three cubes: they differ by more than two fold in what the change removes. Every one of those six is a measured difference and not the machine's scatter: with three runs in each arm, **the two arms' ranges do not touch on any of the six**. ## The output does not move, and the query count does not either Checked before any second was read, on all six arms, three cubes and both gate arms: - **The whole output tree is byte identical to the shipping arm's**: every file, not the mesh alone. Files differing: 0 of 54, 244, 28, 171, 36 and 186. - **The number of queries is unchanged**, exactly, on all six. A pruning cannot change how many questions the caller asks, so this is the check that the change is a pruning and nothing else. - **Resplit's component counts are identical** between the arms on all six, a structural check on a different quantity, read out of the runs' own logs. ## Why it is exactly result preserving The loop keeps `best` and `second` and uses them in one final test, `(second - best) >= margin`. It reads `second` in exactly two places and nowhere else in the function, so only the nearest piece and the truth of that test have to survive, not `second` itself. - A piece nearer than `best` is below any bound we pass, so it is always found. - A piece between `best` and `second` is found, and sets `second` as before. - A piece at or beyond `second` changes nothing either way. The bound reaches the tree squared and is widened by one float step with `nextafterf`, because the caller compares in linear distance and a bound that rounded down could prune a point the loop would have kept. A wider bound only ever adds visits. ## Where the cost was, which is why the bound is the right change Before this, we counted what the gate does to the search with an instrumented build and no clock. Arming the gate multiplies **node visits per query** by 4.80, 7.27 and 6.56 on the three cubes while multiplying the **number of queries** by only 2.75, 1.32 and 1.43. The gate's price is the depth of each query, not how many there are, and that is because most of these queries ask a tree that does not contain the answer: the query point is far from every point of that piece, `best_dist_sq` stays large for the whole descent, and the search walks a large part of the tree to return a distance the caller discards. The bound refuses exactly those at the root. ## What this does not claim Nothing about the other eighteen call sites of `KDTree_nearest`, which this change does not touch. Nothing about arming the gate by default: your own comment explains why it is not armed and this change does not address it. What it does say is that the gate now costs between a third and a half of what it did. ## A further change we have derived and not measured From the second piece the bound could be `min(second, best + margin)`, because the caller needs `second` exactly only while it is below `best + margin`. As it stands, `second` is infinite until two pieces have been asked, so the first two pieces of every point are still searched to the bottom. We have written it and not run it, and it is **not** part of this pull request.
